job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, these are the issues I would flag for the office. Some are direct exceptions or evasion routes; others create uncertainty or leave enforcement dependent on authorities outside this bill.

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel threshold permits fleet splitting.** A company could distribute recovery among vessels that each recover no more than 10,000 metric tons annually. There is no aggregation across vessels, affiliated companies, projects, or coordinated operations.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Substantial extraction below the threshold remains outside the automatic prohibition.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons—or less—per vessel per year is not covered by subparagraph (A), regardless of commercial value or ecological damage. The discretionary provision in subparagraph (B) might capture it, but does not automatically do so.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Per year” is undefined.** The bill does not specify a calendar year, license year, or rolling 12-month period. Operators could exploit the uncertainty through extraction concentrated around annual boundaries.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Tonnage measurement is unspecified.** The text does not establish whether weight means wet material, dry mineral-bearing material, processed minerals, or material recovered before discarding waste. Different accounting methods could materially change whether an operation crosses the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—The vessel-based definition may miss other extraction systems.** Recovery through fixed platforms, seabed installations, or autonomous systems not clearly attributable to a single vessel may fall outside subparagraph (A). The text does not address shared collection systems or transfers among collection and receiving vessels.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” may exclude destructive preparatory activities.** Prospecting, excavation, crushing, seabed clearance, and equipment testing could damage ecosystems without recovering the threshold quantity of minerals. Those activities are not expressly prohibited unless covered by a determination under subparagraph (B).

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—The depth boundary lacks measurement rules.** Mining at exactly 200 meters is excluded, and the bill does not specify the depth datum or treatment of operations spanning the boundary. This creates both a deliberate geographic exclusion and potential measurement disputes.

8. **Section 2(1)(A)—“From the seabed” and “mineral resources” lack precise scope.** The text does not expressly include the subsoil beneath the seabed or identify covered deposits, such as sulfides and cobalt-rich crusts. Although “other mineral resources” is broad, more explicit language would reduce arguments over subsurface extraction and particular materials.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—The responsible “Secretary” is never identified.** Section 6 specifically names the Secretary of State, while section 4 assigns registry functions to NOAA, but neither resolves who makes the ecological-risk determinations. That ambiguity affects the validity and administration of the definition.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—The discretionary provision supplies no decision process or deadline.** It does not require determinations, establish a petition process, specify rulemaking versus individual orders, or state when a determination becomes effective. Operators could continue otherwise uncovered activities while the responsible agency delays or declines to act.

11. **Section 2(1)(B)—“Comparable” ecological risks lack a usable benchmark.** Subparagraph (A) encompasses activities of widely varying scale and impact, yet the bill supplies no criteria for comparing severity, geographic extent, duration, or irreversibility. This creates grounds for challenging individual determinations as inadequately supported or inconsistent.

12. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 5—Open-ended determinations create fair-notice concerns.** “Any activity” could extend well beyond extraction, with no express geographic or commercial limitation in subparagraph (B). Attaching substantial civil penalties and imprisonment to that scope increases the importance of clear, prospective notice and raises vagueness concerns if determinations are insufficiently specific.

13. **Section 2(2)—The domestic-entity definition is incomplete.** “Corporation organized under the laws of a State” does not clearly cover LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or entities organized under federal, tribal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Such entities operating abroad could argue they are not “U.S. persons.”

14. **Section 2(2)—Some individuals with substantial U.S. ties are omitted.** The definition excludes lawful permanent residents and noncitizen U.S. nationals unless they independently qualify as citizens. Their conduct abroad would therefore not be covered on that basis.

15. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries and intermediaries offer an avoidance route.** Foreign-incorporated entities are not U.S. persons merely because Americans own or control them. A U.S. parent’s own participation might still create liability, but ownership alone does not clearly bring the subsidiary’s overseas mining within the prohibition.

16. **Section 3(a)—The geographic and vessel jurisdiction is incomplete.** “In the United States” is undefined, leaving questions about offshore areas, territories, and possessions. There is also no express prohibition on mining by foreign persons aboard U.S.-flagged vessels outside U.S. territory.

17. **Section 3(a)—“Engage in” does not clearly cover the full commercial operation.** Financing, directing, arranging, contracting for, supplying, or materially supporting mining is not expressly addressed. General criminal aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy law may reach some conduct, but the bill does not provide comparably explicit coverage for civil enforcement or indirect participation.

18. **Section 3(a)—There is no import or downstream-commerce prohibition.** Foreign operators beyond the bill’s jurisdiction could continue mining and sell recovered minerals into the United States. Importing, purchasing, processing, and selling those minerals are not expressly prohibited.

19. **Section 3(b)—The exploration-license exception potentially permits commercial extraction.** The exception concerns “mining conducted under an exploration license,” without limiting the quantity, purpose, or duration of mining it exempts. It invites arguments that commercial-scale extraction associated with an old exploration license is protected, although the bill does not itself clearly enlarge what the license authorizes.

20. **Section 3(b)—Qualifying licenses and issuers are unidentified.** The text does not specify a U.S. statutory licensing program or distinguish U.S., foreign, or international licenses. Operators could claim the exception based on instruments Congress did not intend to recognize.

21. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering has no anti-expansion or anti-transfer safeguards.** The exception does not address renewals, extensions, amendments, transfers, successors, enlarged operating areas, or new vessels under an old license. Nor does it expressly require the license to have been valid and in force at enactment.

22. **Section 3(c)—“Environmental assessment” is an unrestricted exemption.** There is no definition, approving authority, required assessment plan, independent oversight, extraction cap, time limit, or restriction on selling recovered minerals. An operator could characterize substantial mining or equipment trials as environmental assessment.

23. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose operations are not addressed.** Activities need only be conducted “for the purpose of environmental assessment,” not exclusively or principally for that purpose. A commercially motivated operation with an assessment component could therefore claim exemption.

24. **Sections 3(b)–(c)—Exception claims lack verification procedures.** The bill does not require advance notice, documentation, or an agency determination before an operator relies on either exception. It also leaves the evidentiary allocation unclear, subject to otherwise applicable civil and criminal rules.

25. **Sections 2(3) and 4—The registry excludes important classes of vessels.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less, and support vessels not themselves equipped for recovery, fall outside the registration requirement. This does **not** exempt them from section 3, but it removes a major monitoring mechanism for potentially prohibited operations.

26. **Section 2(3)—Vessel coverage can turn on uncertain or changeable characteristics.** The bill does not specify the gross-tonnage measurement system or how temporarily installed, removable, or shared recovery equipment affects coverage. It also does not resolve whether particular floating platforms or autonomous vehicles count as vessels.

27. **Section 4(a)—The registry’s jurisdictional reach is unbounded.** “Each covered vessel” contains no U.S.-flag, ownership, location, or port-entry limitation. Read literally, it demands registration of wholly foreign vessels operating abroad, creating enforcement and international-jurisdiction objections; a narrower reading leaves its actual coverage uncertain.

28. **Section 4(a)—Registration duties lack basic implementation details.** There is no registration deadline, express requirement to register before operating, definition of “operator,” or procedure for ownership and operator changes. The bill also does not require disclosure of beneficial owners, controlling entities, licenses, or vessel identifiers needed to connect related operations.

29. **Section 4(b)—Reports need not contain information necessary to prove violations.** “Describing” recovery activities does not expressly require quantities, dates, coordinates, depths, mineral types, transfers, or the basis for claimed exemptions. Quarterly reporting also lacks submission deadlines and may reveal prohibited activity only after substantial damage occurs.

30. **Section 4—Reporting has no independent verification framework.** Operator certification is not backed by express record-retention, audit, inspection, tracking, sampling, or monitoring requirements. NOAA may possess some relevant authority elsewhere, but this bill does not establish a complete verification system.

31. **Section 5—Registry and reporting violations receive no express penalties.** Both penalty provisions apply only to violations of section 3, not section 4. General false-statement law may address some knowingly false submissions, but it does not supply a comprehensive penalty scheme for nonregistration, late reports, or missing records.

32. **Sections 3–5—Enforcement responsibility and powers are not established.** The bill does not identify the lead prohibition-enforcement agency or expressly provide investigative demands, boarding authority, administrative penalty procedures, or referral arrangements. Reliance on existing statutes could leave gaps, especially for overseas conduct.

33. **Section 5—There is no express rapid-stop or restorative remedy.** The bill does not specifically authorize injunctions, vessel detention, mineral seizure or forfeiture, restoration orders, or recovery of response costs. Other law may provide some remedies, but monetary and criminal penalties alone do not ensure that ongoing operations can be stopped promptly or damage addressed.

34. **Section 5(a)—The daily penalty unit is unclear for an annual threshold offense.** If a vessel crosses 10,000 metric tons late in the year, the bill does not say which earlier or later days count as violations. It also does not clearly resolve whether multiple vessels or operations generate separate daily violations.

35. **Section 5(a)—Civil penalties may fail to remove the financial incentive.** The provision supplies a maximum but no express gain-based recovery, mandatory economic-benefit recapture, or security requirement for potentially insolvent operators. A profitable or thinly capitalized operation could treat expected penalties as an operating cost.

36. **Section 5(b)—Criminal enforcement depends on an undefined willfulness standard.** “Willfully” may require proof of awareness of illegality, with its precise meaning determined by context and courts. The bill should clarify the intended mental state rather than leave prosecutors and operators uncertain about what knowledge must be proved.

37. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Civil-penalty timing conflicts with the delayed effective date.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, but section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. This creates uncertainty over the intervening period and potential retroactivity and fair-notice disputes if penalties are sought for conduct before the prohibition takes effect.

38. **Section 8—The 180-day delay permits continued activity.** The bill imposes no interim prohibition or standstill during that period. It also does not expressly bar issuance of new licenses or approvals, although post-enactment exploration licenses would not qualify for section 3(b)’s exception.

39. **Sections 3 and 8—Existing mining laws and authorizations are not reconciled with the prohibition.** The bill does not expressly amend conflicting authorization regimes or direct agencies to deny, suspend, revoke, or modify incompatible permits. A valid permit would not necessarily defeat a later prohibition, but leaving the relationship unstated invites administrative confusion and litigation.

40. **Section 6—The negotiation deadline and required result are unclear.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” could mean beginning efforts, conducting negotiations, or attempting to conclude an agreement by that date. There are no interim milestones, reporting requirements, or express obligations concerning ratification, entry into force, or implementation.

41. **Section 6—“Equivalent” international prohibitions could reproduce the exceptions.** The negotiating mandate points to section 3, which contains the exploration-license and environmental-assessment carveouts. It also specifies no international monitoring, enforcement, compliance, or coverage requirements.

42. **Section 7(a)—The scientific review and reopening standard are underspecified.** No provision commissions or funds the National Academies report, sets its scope or timing, or defines “serious harm.” The text also does not say whether evidence about one method or location could justify ending the prohibition generally.

43. **Sections 7(a)–(b)—The unconditional sunset overrides the safety condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if Congress never finds that mining can proceed without serious harm. Companies can therefore wait out the ban, and the registry and enforcement framework expire with it.

44. **Section 7—Termination provisions do not clearly address transition and surviving duties.** Section 7(a) can end the prohibition while leaving the registry and other provisions operating until the broader sunset, without explaining that relationship. Express savings language should also address accrued liabilities, pending cases, records, and outstanding reporting obligations rather than leave their treatment to general savings law and litigation.

45. **Act-wide—There is no express implementation mandate or funding provision.** The bill assigns NOAA registration and reporting functions without rulemaking deadlines, implementation resources, or a clear broader administrative structure. That omission does not invalidate the prohibition, but could substantially weaken its practical enforcement.

46. **Act-wide—There is no severability clause.** If a court invalidates the discretionary definition, a jurisdictional application, or another provision, the text gives no express direction to preserve the remainder. Courts may sever provisions without such a clause, but including one would reduce avoidable uncertainty.
